articles.title: Miami Sheriff hired friend Israel Reyes’ firm for seizures; deal lets it keep 35% of assets, sparking ethics row as businesses face $45m seizures without charges; revenue jumps 2,325%
articles.summary: Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz’s legal arrangement with her longtime friend, former judge Israel Reyes, has sparked concerns over potential
articles.body: Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz’s legal arrangement with her longtime friend, former judge Israel Reyes, has sparked concerns over potential conflicts of interest and whether law enforcement can profit from property seizures. Under the agreement, Reyes’ law firm can retain up to 35% of assets seized in civil forfeiture cases handled on behalf of the sheriff’s office.The controversy intensified after the office seized more than $45 million in bank accounts and business inventory within two months of signing the agreement. Some affected businesses have not faced criminal charges and are challenging the seizures in court. The arrangement could earn Reyes’ firm more than $10 million from these seizures alone.Under the agreement, Reyes’ law firm receives 30% of assets seized in civil forfeiture cases. If property owners challenge the seizures in court, the firm’s share can increase to 35%, according to the contract. Unlike conventional legal arrangements, the sheriff’s office does not pay Reyes a fixed fee. His compensation is linked to the value of assets recovered.One affected business is SH Americas, described as South Florida’s largest distributor of Samsung phones. The sheriff’s office seized $42.5 million from its bank accounts, leaving the company unable to meet payroll obligations and potentially threatening its operations, according to court filings. The company has not been charged with criminal wrongdoing.Reyes also told a Miami-Dade circuit court that he had identified another $2.6 billion in assets belonging to the parties that could potentially be subject to forfeiture. Successful seizures could earn his firm more than $500 million. However, the court ruled that the identified funds fell outside its jurisdiction and could not currently be seized.Why has the Miami sheriff’s agreement raised ethics concerns?Civil asset forfeiture allows authorities to seize property suspected of being connected to criminal activity without necessarily charging or convicting its owner. Unlike criminal forfeiture, civil proceedings are brought against the property itself, meaning authorities do not always have to establish that the owner committed a crime.Legal experts argue that linking an attorney’s compensation to seized assets could create financial incentives that conflict with the responsibility to pursue justice impartially.Louis Rulli, a practice professor of law at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, expressed concern about the arrangement."The conflict of interest strikes at the foundation of our justice system, of neutrality and of seeking justice," he told WLRN.The lawsuit filed by affected companies also argues that Reyes’ financial interest could influence which seizures are pursued and whether the sheriff’s office chooses to settle cases or continue litigation.Miami-Dade sheriff’s office revenue from forfeitures rises 2,325%The financial implications of asset forfeiture have also drawn attention. Before Cordero-Stutz took office, the existing Miami-Dade Police Department reported $396,000 in revenue from fines and forfeitures. By the following fiscal year, the figure had increased to $9.6 million, marking a 2,325% rise.The money came from cases in which property owners either did not challenge the seizures or lost in court. The sheriff’s office retains the remaining proceeds after deducting the law firm’s share, reporting the money as department revenue rather than transferring it to the state or county treasury.The issue is significant because the sheriff’s office is involved in an ongoing budget dispute with the Miami-Dade Board of County Commissioners. Legal experts fear forfeiture proceeds could allow law enforcement agencies to bypass regular public budgeting and appropriations processes.Rulli warned against allowing police departments to use forfeiture proceeds as an inadequately monitored source of funding."State legislators ought to decide how money obtained through forfeiture should be used. They should not bypass the appropriations process, and that's what guarantees the public that the money's being well spent and it's for appropriate purposes," he said.The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office did not respond to requests by the publication for comment.Miami-Dade judge rejects request to disqualify Israel ReyesCompanies challenging the seizures sought to disqualify Reyes, arguing that his financial interest in the cases creates a conflict of interest and undermines public trust.However, Miami-Dade Circuit Judge Ariana Fajardo Orshan rejected the request. She observed that the sheriff’s office retains control over whether forfeiture cases proceed and must approve settlements."It appears that [Reyes' Law Firm] does not have the discretion to pick and choose which forfeitures will go forward, and therefore does not have the opportunity for example, to choose to bring only those forfeitures that are worth the most money and will result in the greatest profit to the firm," Orshan wrote.The judge noted that the dispute raised a legal question not previously considered by a Florida court in this context. The affected companies are appealing the decision before Florida’s 3rd District Court of Appeal.Attorney Lisandra Guerrero, who represents the companies, criticised the arrangement."Would we accept a police officer collecting a percentage of every traffic ticket he writes? Of course not. His job is to enforce the law, not to make money at the expense of citizens. So why allow it when it comes to lawyers with the power to seize property?" she told WLRN."This practice should be abolished. Policing is not a for-profit enterprise," she added.Who is Israel Reyes? Former police officer and judge has longstanding ties to Miami sheriffReyes joined the Metro-Dade Police Department in 1980 and worked as a homicide detective during the 1980s, investigating organised crime cases. He left the department in 1994 and earned his law degree from Nova Southeastern University before working as a personal injury attorney and in the Dade County State Attorney’s Office.In 2002, Republican Governor Jeb Bush appointed him to a vacant county courthouse seat. A year later, he joined the Eleventh Judicial Circuit, where he served until 2011. He later entered Republican politics, serving as deputy campaign manager for Connie Mack IV’s unsuccessful 2012 US Senate campaign.Reyes also served on influential Florida Bar committees and established R.A. Asset Recovery LLC in 2018, according to state records. Campaign records show he donated $1,000 to Cordero-Stutz’s election campaign in August 2024.How did Rosie Cordero-Stutz become Miami-Dade’s first elected sheriff in nearly 60 years?In January 2025, Republican Rosie Cordero-Stutz was sworn in as Miami-Dade County’s new sheriff, becoming the first person elected to the position in nearly six decades. The position had been abolished by voters in 1966 following widespread corruption allegations. A statewide referendum approved in 2018 restored the requirement for voters to elect their top law enforcement official.During her January 7, 2025, swearing-in ceremony at Miami Dade College’s North Campus, Reyes publicly acknowledged their longstanding friendship."We served together with the Miami-Dade Police Department and you honor me by inviting a has-been judge to come up here and give you and administer the oath," he said.The sheriff’s office assumed control of a budget worth approximately $1.2 billion. About six months later, Cordero-Stutz’s office entered into the controversial agreement with Reyes, bringing their personal and professional ties under scrutiny.Civil asset forfeiture faces criticism across political linesThe Miami-Dade controversy is part of a wider US debate over civil asset forfeiture, which has attracted criticism from both Republicans and Democrats.Tim Sandefur, vice president for legal affairs at the Goldwater Institute, argued that such arrangements could damage public confidence in law enforcement."When you have public resources that are devoted not to hunting down the worst criminals, but instead to hunting down those criminals whose prosecution will be most profitable for the government, that's a really perverse way to do government," he told WLRN.Even conservative US Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas has questioned the constitutionality of civil asset forfeiture. In a 2022 statement, he highlighted how allowing law enforcement agencies to retain seized property could create financial incentives to pursue forfeiture cases. He also warned that the practice disproportionately affects poorer communities, whose members may lack the resources to challenge seizures in court.Florida has previously faced controversies involving forfeiture proceeds. In 2015, the US Department of Justice forced the city of Bal Harbour to return $4 million seized by its police department after investigators found that the money had been used for lavish expenses, including first-class flights.The Miami-Dade agreement has renewed questions about financial incentives behind civil asset forfeiture, public accountability and whether private lawyers should receive a percentage of property seized using government powers.You use AI every day. articles.title: Somali Uber driver left with life-threatening injuries as police investigate possible hate crime
articles.summary: An Uber driver was “fighting for his life” Monday following an attack that Minnesota police are investigating as a potential hate crime against the Somali American man, authorities said.
articles.body: An Uber driver was “fighting for his life” Monday following an attack that Minnesota police are investigating as a potential hate crime against the Somali American man, authorities said. The driver was a “victim of a serious assault” on Saturday, leaving him with “life-threatening injuries that investigators believe were inflicted by a passenger in the vehicle,” according to a Hopkins police statement. Hopkins is a city in Hennepin County, just outside Minneapolis. “Investigators are examining all available evidence and considering all potential motives, including whether bias played a role in the assault,” Hopkins Police Chief Brent Johnson said. Police did not immediately identify the driver. The Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) and the victim’s family identified him as Somali American Mohamed Yusuf. “A passenger asked his name, told him he didn’t like that name and then he attacked him,” said Suleiman Adan, deputy executive director of CAIR Minnesota. The attacker tried to strangle the driver and then used the victim’s car to try running over him, according to Jaylani Hussein, executive director of CAIR Minnesota. “This is one of the most heinous attacks that we have ever seen,” Hussein said. Uber said it was shocked by the attack. “We banned the rider from the Uber platform and are keeping the driver and his loved ones in our thoughts as we continue to support law enforcement with their investigation,” the company said in a statement. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison reposted a Somali news story identifying the victim with a picture of him in the hospital. “There will be accountability for this horrific crime,” Ellison added. “My heart breaks for Mohamed, his loved ones, and our Somali and Muslim communities apparently targeted by this assault. Everyone should feel safe and be safe in Minnesota — no exceptions. Hate and violence have no place here.” Minnesota has become a hub for Somali immigration, and President Donald Trump has told Minnesotans to “fight back” against this community of recently arrived Americans. The president has repeatedly verbally attacked Somalis, as well as Rep. Ilhan Omar, who was born in Somalia. Federal agents searched the lawmaker’s home last month in an inquiry of possible irregularities in her immigration process. Omar has denied any allegations and said she feels “confident in my truth.” Trump’s attacks on Somali immigrants in Minnesota come in the wake of reports last year about dozens of people of Somali descent who were convicted of fraud schemes. Since then, Trump has called Somalis “crooks” and referred to Somalia as “filthy, dirty, disgusting, dirty.” Somali immigrants are living in “fear, hatred, bigotry and demonization” that’s “come from the highest office of the land,” according to Hussein. “This rhetoric has built an environment that we are living in today, an environment which we believe has created this heinous attack that took place on Saturday night here in Minnesota,” he added. Hopkins Mayor Patrick Hanlon asked the public for time to allow department investigators to do their work. “We ask for the community’s patience and understanding as investigators work diligently to determine the full circumstances surrounding this case,” the mayor said. “All of our investigators have been working non-stop to follow up on evidence and determine the facts.”

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV hit in the face by flying rosary during farewell Mass in Peru, video shows
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV was struck near the eye by a rosary tossed at his popemobile in Lima, Peru, video shows, but the pontiff continued the farewell Mass.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV appeared to be struck near the eye by a rosary Monday as he reached out to catch prayer beads tossed toward his popemobile ahead of a massive farewell Mass in Lima, Peru. Video shows the 71-year-old pontiff wincing, clutching his face and rubbing his eye after the beads appeared to hit him as his vehicle slowed near the altar at Las Palmas Air Base. Leo showed no obvious signs of injury and continued with the Mass, marking the end of his six-day visit to Peru and a grueling 12-day tour of South America, Reuters reported. An estimated 1.5 million people attended the farewell Mass, where the pope thanked Peruvians for their hospitality and reaffirmed his deep connection to the country, which he considers his second homeland. POPE LEO DRAWS STAGGERING 800,000 FAITHFUL TO HEART OF PARIS FOR MASSIVE OUTDOOR MASS "I wish to confirm you in faith and charity and assure you that I will always carry you with me. Yes, the Peruvian people are my people, too," he told the crowd. The incident came as the pontiff traveled through crowds of faithful Catholics in his popemobile, a specially designed vehicle equipped with security features to protect the leader of the Roman Catholic Church. Leo has previously been seen catching dolls, flags and other gifts tossed by worshipers as he travels in his popemobile. During an appearance in St. Peter's Square, he even accepted pizza offered by fellow Chicagoans, according to Reuters. At another event in Rome, the pope accidentally struck a Vatican cameraman riding behind him while reaching for a flying gift, prompting him to apologize to the operator. HOW A CHICAGO BANK TELLER ONCE HUNG UP ON POPE LEO, WHO REPORTEDLY CALLED FROM THE VATICAN TO ADJUST NUMBER Born Robert Prevost in Chicago in 1955, Leo became the first American pope in May 2025, when 133 cardinals gathered in the Sistine Chapel and elected him to lead the world's 1.4 billion Catholics. Stepping onto the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica before thousands of cheering faithful, he had greeted the crowd with the words, "Peace be with you." He also paid tribute to Peru at the time, since he spent decades serving as a missionary and bishop there before becoming pontiff. POPE LEO XIV SEEN FOR FIRST TIME SINCE LUNG CANCER SURGERY AMID MAJOR RECOVERY MILESTONE Switching to speaking in Spanish at the event on Monday, Leo told the crowd, "I would particularly like to say hello to my compatriots from Peru. It was a great pleasure for me to work in Peru." Pope Leo's South American tour began in Uruguay and carried on through Argentina before ending in Peru. The trip included 12 flights, two helicopter rides and nine Masses, as well as 36 speeches. articles.title: Neighbours' shock after WW2 mortar found in Doncaster garage
articles.summary: Army bomb disposal experts were called to the street in Doncaster on Friday 13 November.
articles.body:
Residents of a street which had to be evacuated after a World War Two mortar shell was found during a house clearance have said they were "shocked" at the unexpected discovery.

An Army bomb disposal unit had to be called to safely detonate the device after it was discovered at a property on Robin Hood Crescent in Edenthorpe, Doncaster, on Friday 13 November.

Neighbours said until police told them to leave their homes they had no idea the ordnance was inside the garage of the semi-detached property which had belonged to an elderly couple.

The property, which had recently been sold, was being cleared after an Army veteran and his wife had moved out.

Next door neighbour Dave Milnes, 55, said he had been friends with the man as they had both served in the armed forces.

"We had a good bond and we both helped to build the Edenthorpe village war memorial in 2015," he said.

"I'd seen a load of old radio equipment inside the garage before, but I had no idea about any ordnance."

Milnes, who served in the Royal Navy, added that he and his neighbour would often go to Remembrance services together.

He explained that the man and his wife had been "a lovely couple - they moved out because of illness".

The mortar had been found under a board during the house clearance, he said.

"He had a lot of old World War Two radios, so possibly the mortar was given to him as a memento and he forgot about it," he added.

"I was a bit worried that it would all blow up as I've only just had a new floor put down."

Another resident, Mark Szpak, said he had heard about the evacuation while he was at work.

He described the neighbour as an "old soldier" to whom he had regularly spoken and who had been a driver for the Army while serving in Germany.

Meanwhile, Rachel Sayer, 25, another resident of Robin Hood Crescent, said the afternoon had turned "very strange" after she was told to leave her property.

"I phoned my mum and told her and she was a bit panicky," she said.

"I was out of the house for two to three hours."

The road was finally reopened at about 17:00 GMT after an Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit had carried out a controlled detonation of the device.

articles.title: 2 kids, 6 years, 1 sound machine: Why I’m still obsessed with the Hatch Baby
articles.summary: I’ve used the Hatch Baby sound machine and night light with both my kids for nearly six years. Here’s why it’s the one product I tell new moms to buy.
articles.body: When I became a mom, I didn’t just get a baby. I got a membership card. Nobody tells you this part, but becoming a parent automatically signs you up for a club. If you’re lucky, the other members show up right away. Mine did. Fellow moms swooped in to listen when I needed to vent, to share the hacks that got them through the newborn fog, and to tell me which products — strollers, car seats, baby bags — would actually make my life easier and which ones I could skip. Now that I’m a mom of two, I’ve moved from new recruit to the welcoming committee. A few weeks after a friend tells me she’s pregnant, she always texts: “Okay, what do I actually need?” It’s a fair question. There’s an overwhelming amount of baby gear out there, and it’s hard to know what’s essential and what’s just clever marketing. I have a long answer about swaddles and bottles and which gadgets to pass on. But I always tell them to put one thing at the top of their registry: a Hatch Baby. I don’t recommend much baby gear without a caveat. Most of what we bought lasted a few months before it ended up in the basement or the donation pile. The Hatch Baby is the exception. My daughter is nearly 6 and my son is nearly 2, and there’s one in each of their rooms — it has been part of our bedtime routine since the first week of each of their lives. Not only does it help them sleep better, it makes my life easier, too. And that is exactly why it is one of the products I talk about most often. Not familiar with this genius device? Read more about it below. The Hatch Baby is a combination sound machine and night light that allows you to control the volume, sound and light right on the device. Then, the Hatch app helps with setup and advanced features like schedules, favorites and customization. The available sounds include white noise, ocean, rain, fan and thunderstorm, plus lullabies like “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.” The light settings are also customizable, so you can choose color and brightness. It also works as a sleep trainer for older babies and toddlers, using light cues to show them when it’s time for bed and when it’s okay to get up. For example, you can set it to stay red during sleep hours and turn green when it is okay for them to leave their room in the morning. What sets the Hatch Baby apart from a basic sound machine is the sleep help that comes with it. Hatch gives parents the option to chat with certified sleep consultants and sleep guides. That support comes through Hatch+. Three months of Hatch+ are included in your purchase — after that it costs $5 a month or $50 for a year. While you don’t need a subscription for the sound machine and night light to work, Hatch+ is needed to access the full premium library and additional features, such as premium stories, songs, dynamic lights and sleep-support content. Every purchase also comes with free shipping and returns, a 30-night bedside trial, and a 1-year product warranty. Who is the Hatch Baby for? The Hatch Baby is for every expecting parent, and it’s what I’d put at the top of any baby registry. It’s especially helpful if you have a noisy home, whether that’s caused by a barking dog, a busy street or an older sibling who’s still awake. Down the road, it’s a lifesaver for toddlers and preschoolers who wake up before the sun. It makes a great baby shower gift, because the recipient will use it for years. What I love about the Hatch Baby It drowns out my very loud dog We have a French bulldog who barks a lot. At delivery trucks, at the doorbell, at nothing at all. I was adamant that nap time would not feel like a game of chance. The Hatch’s white noise has been our best defense. It creates a steady wall of sound that muffles the barking, so my kids stay asleep instead of popping up every time the dog decides he needs to yell at the wind blowing. It grows up with them The best gear changes jobs as your kid grows, and this one does exactly that. When my kids were babies, the Hatch Baby was a dim light for middle-of-the-night feeds and a sound machine to help them settle. In the toddler years, it became a sleep trainer. When transitioning my daughter out of her crib and into a regular bed, I create a new schedule on her Hatch. Thirty minutes before bed, the sound machine turns down at a quiet level. This is her signal that it is time to start winding down. Then, at bedtime, the light turns red and stays that way until she is allowed to get out of the bed the next morning. When it is okay for her to get out of bed, the light turns green. Having these signals has helped her understand what is expected of her and when, and she loves the routine of it. I can change it from my phone Any parent knows that the creak of a bedroom door can undo an hour of rocking. Being able to turn up the volume, dim the light or switch it off from my phone is game changing. It tells my daughter when she can get out of bed This is the feature I talk about most. Little kids can’t read a clock, but they understand colors. I set a schedule in the app so my daughter’s light glows one color when it’s time to sleep and changes to another when she’s allowed to leave her room in the morning. It turned our mornings from a negotiation into a routine. She knows the rule, the light keeps track of it and I’m no longer the bad guy. Because the schedule runs every day on its own, I set it once and only adjust it now and then when her bedtime changes. A few things to know about the Hatch Baby If you haven’t picked up on it by now, I will say it plainly: I love the Hatch Baby. But, as with any product, there are a few things you should note before you decide to get one for yourself. It needs an outlet. The Hatch Baby has no battery, so it has to stay plugged in. That also means it won’t keep running during a power outage.The app is necessary. Power, volume, sound and light can be controlled on the device itself. But schedules and customization happen in the Hatch app. I also find the app to be an easier way to switch the sound and light, even though those things can technically be done on the device.Hatch+ is optional. Three months of Hatch+ come with the device. After that, you don’t need to pay anything for the sound machine, light and bedtime and wake-up cues to keep working. A subscription, however, gets you access to extras like premium stories, songs and sleep-support content. The verdict I’ve told a lot of friends what to buy for their new babies, and the advice has changed over the years. This one recommendation hasn’t. The Hatch Baby has been there for every bedtime, every early morning and every nap the dog tried to ruin, across nearly six years and two kids. It made our nights calmer and our mornings later. articles.title: JD Vance says he and Trump still 'don't know' whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy
articles.summary: JD Vance says intelligence on whether Alice Huang spied for China points in different directions, as Nvidia faces national security scrutiny over chips.

articles.title: United Airlines says technology issue resolved after ‘widespread system outage’
articles.summary: United Airlines flights were stuck on tarmacs as pilots reported a companywide IT issue preventing takeoff data, days after the nationwide FAA ground stop.
articles.body: United Airlines said Monday it resolved a technology issue that delayed departing flights, marking another disruption for travelers just days after a nationwide FAA ground stop. "We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures. While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights," United Media Relations told Fox News Digital. "There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue," the airline added. Earlier Monday, passengers reported being unable to take off, with one saying their flight was returning to the gate because the crew could not obtain performance data needed for departure. FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP United initially acknowledged a widespread outage in a response to a passenger on X. "We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible," United’s official X account wrote in response to a passenger. The airline apologized and urged travelers to monitor their flight status through the United app or its website. Its response did not identify the cause or provide an estimated restoration time. One passenger reported being stuck on the tarmac, saying crews could not clear planes for takeoff because they could not connect to a weight system. Another social media user said their flight was returning to the gate after the pilot announced a company wide IT issue that left the crew "unable to get performance data for takeoff." "Pilot just announced ALL of United Airlines has a company wide IT issue," the user wrote. "We’re going back to the gate." Another passenger reported a similar announcement while waiting for departure. "Waiting to take off, on the runway, and the pilot just said we can’t take off because United is experiencing a system-wide computer outage," the user wrote. AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS The X account @theATCapp also posted that it was receiving reports of a systemwide IT outage affecting the airline. United’s response acknowledged a widespread outage but did not confirm the passengers’ descriptions of the affected systems. The number of flights and airports affected was not immediately clear. Flight-tracking service Flightradar24 reported that United’s mainline departures were beginning to resume. "We are seeing mainline departures resuming in the last few minutes," the service posted on X. At Los Angeles International Airport, Fox News correspondent Max Gorden spoke with several passengers at the United counter who were able to check in for their flights. However, an agent showed Gorden her United mobile device, which appeared to be experiencing technical problems. The outage comes after a telecommunications failure prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to issue a nationwide ground stop Friday, Nov. 13. The restriction was later lifted, but airlines faced lingering delays and cancellations as they worked to restore their schedules. Following Friday’s ground stop, United CEO Scott Kirby praised the FAA’s decision to halt flights and thanked employees and customers for their patience. He also called for better technology and full staffing to help prevent future outages. Kirby said he had spoken directly with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford and aviation leaders from both parties in Congress about the impact on United’s passengers and employees. "This moment must be a call to action," Kirby said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital. "It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation’s Air Traffic Control system now." Kirby said lawmakers from both parties were committed to modernizing the system while holding the FAA accountable. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There was no immediate confirmation that United’s outage Monday was connected to Friday’s FAA disruption. This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title: Guatemala ramps up security operations following declaration of state of siege
articles.summary: GUATEMALA CITY (AP) — Guatemala’s interior and defense ministers on Monday inspected security operations in two departments bordering Honduras, days after Pr...
articles.body:
GUATEMALA CITY (AP) — Guatemala's interior and defense ministers on Monday inspected security operations in two departments bordering Honduras, days after President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency to curb drug-related violence in the Central American country.

The decree, announced on Saturday, suspends for 30 days several constitutional rights, including freedom of movement and assembly, and allows security forces to disperse groups by force, make arrests and enter homes without warrants.

Interior Minister Marco Antonio Villeda said Monday that the emergency measure also targets groups allegedly linked to drug trafficking that are involved in illegal jade and gold mining in the region.

"We are carrying out a series of coordinated and planned actions with the Defense Ministry and the public prosecutor's office. We have a plan that we will execute over 30 days," Villeda said.

Defense Minister Henry Sáenz said authorities are "establishing territorial control through checkpoints on routes and patrols along roads bordering Honduras."

This area in the eastern part of Guatemala has been the scene of a wave of violence over the past three months.

On Sept. 27, an armed attack left eight people dead in the municipality of Huité, in the department of Zacapa.

Initially, the army claimed the attack involved clashes between organized crime groups; however, days later, it announced that 107 military personnel had been placed at the disposal of the authorities to determine their potential involvement in the massacre, which claimed the lives of three women, including a young girl.

The prosecutor's office is investigating whether the army's actions were linked to the detention of suspected drug traffickers.

Separately, on Nov. 7, Congressman Julio César Portillo Paz and three members of the National Civil Police — who were part of his security detail — were gunned down by armed men in broad daylight in the municipality of Río Hondo, also in Zacapa.

Early on Friday morning, five people were killed in the same department. According to preliminary investigations, armed men arrived in several vehicles at a small village and abducted a man, whose whereabouts remain unknown. They then killed his mother, two brothers and two friends at the scene.

Also on Friday, the U.S. State Department designated three local drug-trafficking groups as terrorist organizations for financing violence and crime in the region. Among those designated are two family clans — Los Lorenzanas and Los Mendoza — which, according to authorities, maintain deep ties to Mexican drug cartels and operate within the area.

articles.title: Pakistan’s imprisoned ex-leader Imran Khan appeals for urgent medical care
articles.summary: ISLAMABAD — Pakistan’s imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed Monday to the country’s top judges, seeking their help in getting urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife and alleging that authorities had failed to implement an earlier court order to transfer him to a hospital in the capital, Islamabad.
articles.body: ISLAMABAD — Pakistan’s imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed Monday to the country’s top judges, seeking their help in getting urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife and alleging that authorities had failed to implement an earlier court order to transfer him to a hospital in the capital, Islamabad. In an open letter and conveyed to the judges through his lawyer, Khan said his blood pressure had risen sharply and that doctors had warned him he was at risk of a brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest. According to the letter released to the media by Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party and lawyer Salman Safdar, the former premier said that his wife, Bushra Bibi, also needed further eye surgery and could permanently lose her sight without it. Khan has been in prison since 2023 after being convicted in a graft case. He was removed from office in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. Despite his legal troubles, Khan remains a central and popular figure in Pakistan, and the PTI wants his release. Khan’s wife is also serving a prison term on graft charges. Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, a Cabinet minister, disputed Khan’s account, saying he was receiving regular medical care and accusing him of seeking political advantage. In a post on X, Chaudhry said Khan has been taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad eight times for examinations, where his health and blood pressure were found to be satisfactory. He said Khan received meals of his choice and had access to books and television. The government was responsible for ensuring Khan’s medical care and protecting his legal rights, as it was for every prisoner, Chaudry said. The latest development comes days after authorities allowed Khan’s lawyers to see him at the prison. “Today, I ask only that my wife and I be treated,” he said according to the letter. “I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive.” The letter was addressed to the chief justices of Pakistan’s Supreme Court and other courts. “I appeal to Your Lordships, on the most basic grounds of human compassion: give me justice before it is too late,” Khan said. Earlier this year, Safdar, Khan’s lawyer, told the Supreme Court that the former premier had lost roughly 85% of vision in his right eye. The government at the time denied the claim, and one of Khan’s sisters said his eyesight had significantly improved following medical treatment, which authorities say is ongoing. The government of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has said that Khan isn’t being held under a government order, but as a “convicted prisoner” serving sentences imposed by the courts following judicial proceedings. The government has rejected allegations that Khan was being held in solitary confinement or denied contact with his family, saying Khan had received more than 900 visits since his imprisonment in 2023.

articles.title: French troops secretly deployed inside Ukraine as ex-NATO chief praises Macron's 'guts'
articles.summary: President Emmanuel Macron's France reportedly runs covert "Volia" mission training Ukrainian troops as Zelenskyy holds fresh peace talks with the US.
articles.body: French troops have reportedly been operating secretly inside Ukraine for months, training Ukrainian forces and maintaining military equipment and, as NATO experts claim, President Emmanuel Macron is taking a more assertive role in supporting Kyiv against Russia. The covert mission, codenamed "Volia," has operated since at least summer 2026, with small teams of French military personnel deployed on short-term assignments under the supervision of a French general, Radio France Internationale (RFI) reported Monday. Agence France-Presse (AFP) also separately reported the French military presence, citing sources who said the troops were not involved in combat. UKRAINE HITS PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE IN RECORD DRONE BLITZ AS KREMLIN TELLS LAWMAKERS TO PREPARE FOR 'VICTORY' The reports come as the United States and European allies pursue renewed, high-stakes negotiations to end Russia's war in Ukraine, raising questions about the extent of Western military involvement in the conflict. Former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Gen. Philip Breedlove meanwhile, told Fox News Digital that the covert French mission sends a powerful message to Russian President Vladimir Putin at a critical juncture for Europe. "The timing of what the French are doing and their announcement of what they're doing is important," Breedlove said. "A very powerful NATO ally — both politically and militarily — is making a strong statement of support for Ukraine. "And this is what Mr. Putin needs to see. He needs to look across the line and see that the Western alliances, NATO in this case, are standing up for Ukraine." "It's very important to remember that if Mr. Putin stops fighting, this war ends. If Ukraine stops fighting, Ukraine ends," he said before adding that this is "an existential war that we in the West need to support to the appropriate conclusion." UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS The French mission reportedly focuses on training Ukrainian troops and maintaining French-supplied equipment, including CAESAR self-propelled howitzers, Mirage 2000 fighter jets and precision-guided missiles. French personnel have rotated between France, Poland and Ukraine under what RFI described as a "light and flexible" operational structure. French newspaper Le Monde separately reported Monday that personnel had also worked alongside Ukrainian intelligence units on observation missions closer to the front lines. The deployment would mark a significant step in Macron's military support for Kyiv despite repeated Russian warnings against Western troop involvement. "I cannot imagine the French military would deploy into Ukraine without their commander-in-chief approving it," Breedlove said of Macron while noting that Western military training missions inside Ukraine predate Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. "It's not new to have training facilities inside of Ukraine. But almost all of them, and almost everyone, left Ukraine when the war started, which I disagree with, but that was the decision," he said. Breedlove also pointed to the Yavoriv military training facility in western Ukraine, where NATO countries helped train Ukrainian forces following Russia's initial intervention in 2014. "In 2014, we had a training area called Yavoriv," he said. "We had a large facility of NATO training ability there, and we trained Ukrainians all the time. When the war started back in 2014 — remembering this is a 12-year-long war — most of those nations left, to include the United States." RIOT-TORN FRANCE STRUGGLES WITH CHAOS AT HOME AS MACRON EYES MILITARY MISSION THOUSANDS OF MILES AWAY "I would congratulate and thank France for having the guts to go in there and do what we all should be doing to help Ukraine fight this illegal, immoral, inhumane war that Russia is persecuting the Ukrainian people with," Breedlove said. RFI reported that French lawmakers had not been formally informed of the deployment, with authorities maintaining that parliamentary approval was unnecessary because the mission did not involve combat operations. France has trained approximately 25,000 Ukrainian soldiers in France and Poland since 2023, according to Le Monde. Macron raised the possibility of sending Western military instructors into Ukraine in 2024, prompting concerns among allies, including the United States and Germany, about a potential escalation with Moscow. France has also helped lead efforts to establish a multinational force to support a potential postwar security arrangement for Ukraine. Russia has repeatedly opposed the presence of Western troops in Ukraine, while Putin has characterized Western military assistance to Kyiv as evidence of a proxy conflict between Russia and NATO. TRUMP PUSHED NATO TO SPEND BIG — NOW COMES THE HARDER QUESTION: CAN EUROPE ACTUALLY FIGHT? The reports surfaced as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced fresh talks Monday with American and European representatives aimed at ending the war. Zelenskyy said Ukrainian officials held online discussions with U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, along with European representatives, about prospects for a negotiated settlement with Russia. The Ukrainian leader also warned that intelligence indicated Russia was preparing major strikes against Ukrainian targets Monday evening, overnight and Tuesday. Breedlove suggested that France's reported mission could now encourage other NATO members to further expand their support for Ukraine. "I think that there are more than a few NATO nations that would love to be in there helping," he said. "They're the ones that call themselves the Eastern Front, those nations that border Russia in various parts of the eastern flank of NATO." "And so I'm sure there are other nations that want to do this, but they're looking for leadership to go do it," he said. articles.title: Suneung: Taking Korea's toughest exam from behind bars
articles.summary: Eleven convicts at the Mandela Boys' School will be among the thousands of young Koreans taking the country's hardest exam, the Suneung.
articles.body:
Students intently focus on maths formulas written on a board before lowering their heads and taking notes as the teacher works through a sum.

The teacher's voice and the scratch of pens fill the room.

At first glance, this could be any classroom in South Korea.

But thick metal bars cover the windows and the students are wearing blue prison uniforms and rubber shoes emblazoned with the words "Korea Correctional Service".

This is Mandela Boys' School, an education facility for young prisoners inside the Seoul Southern Correctional Institution in Guro, south-west Seoul. In South Korea, young people who are sentenced to imprisonment by a criminal court must serve their time in prison.

"The boys here have committed serious offences and received criminal sentences," Jeong Yeo-gyeong, a correctional officer in the Korea Correctional Service's social reintegration division, told the BBC.

"As well as theft, there is a high proportion of serious offences, including violence, bodily injury, sexual violence and robbery."

But by opening educational institutes like Mandela, authorities are hoping to give these young offenders a chance to better their lives after they serve out their sentences.

Opened by the justice ministry in March 2023, it allows boys who were aged 17 and under when their sentences became final to prepare for school equivalency exams as well as the Suneung - the country's notoriously difficult university entrance examination - while still serving their sentences.

Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.

Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.

The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.

A total of 551,864 people have applied to take this year's Suneung on 19 November.

Around 30 prisoners are enrolled in the Suneung preparation class at Mandela Boys' School, and 11 of them have applied to take this year's exam.

Park Soo-young (not his real name), a 17-year-old inmate, has been at the Mandela Boys' Suneung preparation class for two months and hopes to study social welfare.

He tells the BBC that he had dreams of becoming a police officer before committing the crime that landed him behind bars.

He says he could not bring himself to look properly at his mother during his trial. When he turned towards her after his sentence was announced, she was crying.

"Seeing her like that, I broke down too. I wondered how I was going to live from then on, and how I could look after my mother, who was on her own. I think I kept crying for about a week while I was in the detention centre."

Looking back on his offence, he says he feels "very ashamed that I couldn't control that impulse". If he could meet his younger self, he would tell him: "Control that impulse. If you do, everything will be different."

"I'd grab myself by the collar and shake myself as I said it."

He hopes the Suneung and university will offer him a chance to start again.

"Once I'm out, I need to cut ties with the friends and people I used to know and start a new life. I think university is the only way to do that. Going to university would let me leave the area where I used to live, move somewhere else and start something new. That's why I began studying again."

But he describes beginning Suneung preparation as "a struggle every day".

"But the teachers don't let anything slip past. They keep helping us until we understand. If I don't understand something, I put my hand up and they come over and explain it.

Sometimes, if I've missed something, I keep working at it on my own. If I still can't get it, I ask the students next to me to explain," he said.

Park's day begins at 06:30 with a morning check by prison officers. He starts memorising English vocabulary and working through Korean reading passages early in the morning.

"I learn English words whenever I can, even before breakfast. From 07:00, I work through a Korean passage, something like literature or speech. We have to come down to the classroom at 08:00, so we have another check and then come down for lessons."

During breaks, students make calls to their families or leave the classroom for scheduled visits. In the evening, they return for supervised study. Once the day's activities are over, they must go back to their cells together.

Park says he studies until 22:00 before finishing for the day. If he wants to study longer hours, he needs permission from a prison officer.

But even if gets a good result this year, Park will not be allowed to leave prison and attend university straight away. He is only due to be released in 2028, but plans to use this exam as experience and continue studying next year.

"This time, I want to experience how the Suneung works and how competitive it is. Then, next year, I'll work hard from the start so I can get in the year after that."

Some former students from Mandela Boys' School have managed to get into university, according to the justice ministry.

Others have continued their studies after leaving prison, including by enrolling in residential exam preparation academies.

The inmates are taught by a team of seven prison officers, all of whom hold teaching certificates. Each is responsible for a subject.

Visiting instructors provide classes in the humanities, arts and sport, while university student volunteers help with learning. Professional psychological counselling is also available.

Park Min-yong, who applied to work here in 2023, teaches science. And alongside Suneung lessons, he works with the students' to change their habits and behaviour.

One thing he often tells them is that they need to "learn how to become adults".

He believes that while studying in itself does not necessarily turn inmates away from a life of crime, the experience of having worked hard at something: staying with a concept that makes little sense, revisiting a wrong answer and continuing even when grades do not improve straight away, is valuable in itself.

"Studying properly means pushing yourself to your limits, and that takes considerable stamina and patience," he says.

"Whether they chose to do it or not, the experience of persevering, enduring and not giving up easily may help them to some extent when they face the difficulties of life after release."

He says the material they encounter while preparing for the Suneung also gives them new things to think about.

Korean reading passages cover literature, society, science and philosophy. Students have to consider a character's perspective, examine the evidence behind an argument and understand unfamiliar concepts. They also encounter explanations that differ from their own and have to reconsider what they think.

"They gradually learn that it's not just about their own personal view - that these concepts and relationships have been developed through a shared understanding among many people," Park said.

Park says students sometimes cheat in classroom tests even while he is watching.

"They cheat as if it's nothing. They give each other answers, even when I'm watching them. Some repeat it after being told off. There may be an element of doing it deliberately, but often they haven't thought it through. They don't think about the impact their actions or words could have on others."

The boys also have a strong desire for recognition, he says.

"It's all the time. 'Look how much I've done. Look how much my grades have improved. I've done this much - haven't I done well?' They're always like that. They're hungry for it."

Not everyone agrees with this initiative though.

One criticism is that young people who have not committed crimes also face fierce competition for university places: so there is some anger that the state provides offenders with separate education and opportunities to prepare for this exam.

Father Jeong Min-ha, of the Archdiocese of Seoul's correctional ministry committee, worked with Seoul Southern Correctional Institution from September 2023 until last year.

"Studying gives them a sense of achievement and time to look seriously at their own lives. That's why I think it matters. I think that is the most important part of rehabilitation."

Park recalls a student who had done well at the school but later returned to prison.

"He was doing well when he left, but in the end he came back. So something went wrong. I'd hoped he would carry on with what he'd been doing here, but he couldn't. That's disappointing."

According to the justice ministry's 2026 corrections statistical yearbook, 35.5% of prisoners aged under 20 who were released in 2021 were imprisoned again within three years. That was about 1.7 times the overall rate of 21.2%, and the highest of any age group.

But Park hopes the students will continue learning after they leave prison. "We don't know what the outcome will be," he says.

"They say the way to clear a glass of dirty water is to keep pouring clean water into it, rather than trying to remove each bit of dirt. I hope they fill their minds with good things, learn to use their energy and intellect in the right way, and put that learning into practice at the right time and place."

articles.title: Aged 16-24 and looking for work? Use our look-up to find out which areas have the most jobs
articles.summary: How many jobs are there where you live and in which sectors are you most likely to find an opening?
articles.body:
If you're one of the nearly one million people aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet" - then you might be wondering where to start.

Under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work, a major review aimed at cutting the number of Neets will say.

But how many jobs are there where you live and in which sectors are you most likely to find an opening?

There is no official measure of how many vacancies are suitable for young people, but across the whole economy there were 691,000 jobs available in the July to September period this year, which is the lowest number since early 2021.

The Covid pandemic led to huge swings in the number of job vacancies available as companies reacted to shutdowns and then reopened as restrictions were lifted.

Stripping out the fluctuations seen during the pandemic, the number of vacancies is now at its lowest level for 12 years.

Apprenticeships have often been a way for people to get their first taste of employment.

In England the number of people starting apprenticeships has risen in recent years, although this has been driven by an increase in those aged 25 and over after schemes for older workers were fully rolled out in 2008.

The number of people aged 24 and under starting apprenticeships in England in 2025 was 172,230, down from a recent peak of 291,300 in 2012.

Where you live will often have a big impact on your ability to find a job.

We have used online job adverts to help identify the number of vacancies suitable for young people in the area they live, relative to the size of the local population.

The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank used AI to help identify the jobs, which were broadly defined as roles requiring relatively low experience or education.

According to its analysis, South Oxfordshire had 387 suitable vacancies per 1,000 18 to 24-year-olds in the area - the most of any local authority. Rotherham had the least, at 53 per 1,000.

Use this tool to check out the situation in your area. The data for London is only available for the region as a whole and is not broken down by individual councils.

Which sectors have the most entry-level jobs?

Even if there are jobs available in your area, you might not find one in the sector you want to work in.

The sector with the highest average number of entry-level vacancies in the year to October was teaching, with most of those jobs being for teaching assistants, learning support and cover supervisor roles, according to jobs website Adzuna.

The next largest was hospitality and catering, traditionally an area where younger people get their first experience of work.

Adzuna, a major online jobs website, includes adverts for full-time roles marked as entry-level, those asking for up to two years' experience, graduate roles, internships and apprenticeships.

Accounting and finance had the third-highest number of job openings.

Figures on salaries for vacancies can be patchy because many employers do not include them in job adverts.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently urged businesses to start publishing salaries ahead of plans to make pay details compulsory in adverts .

Only about 40% of Adzuna's jobs data for the year to October stated a salary, although that figure varies widely by sector.

Here are the average salaries for jobs in the sectors with the largest number of entry-level jobs, according to Adzuna. The highest average salary is £30,530 in engineering, while social care has the lowest at £25,880.

articles.title: Ties with Asean crucial for India's Act East Policy: PM
articles.summary: As he arrived in Manila for the India-Asean and East Asia Summit meetings, PM Modi said his visit will impart new energy to India's partnership with the
articles.body: As he arrived in Manila for the India-Asean and East Asia Summit meetings, PM Modi said his visit will impart new energy to India's partnership with the political and economic union of southeast Asian nations and reinforce the collective commitment to a peaceful, prosperous and resilient Indo-Pacific.Modi attended a dinner hosted by Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr soon after his arrival, and ahead of the main multilateral and bilateral engagements Tuesday. While no bilateral meet with US President Trump had been scheduled till late Monday, official sources confirmed the Quad leaders' summit would take place Tuesday evening.Trump is expected to spend only a few hours in Manila, before taking off for Shenzhen in China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting. Modi will attend a groundbreaking ceremony at a gurudwara Tuesday morning before participating in the 23rd Asean-India summit.In his departure statement in Delhi, Modi said India's relationship with Asean countries is at the heart of India's Act East Policy and occupies a central place in its MAHASAGAR vision. "Our ties, rooted in centuries of civilisational exchanges, have grown into a dynamic partnership spanning trade, connectivity, maritime security, technology and people-to-people relations," said Modi, who did not mention Quad in his statement.All eyes on Quad as Modi to hold bilateral with MarcosModi also said that at the ASEAN-India Summit, he was looking forward to working with fellow leaders to build on the progress of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and give further momentum to the shared aspirations for growth, connectivity and prosperity.The PM also spoke about the East Asia Summit, saying it provides an important platform for dialogue on regional and global challenges. "I look forward to exchanging views with participating leaders on strengthening peace, stability and cooperation in the Indo-Pacific," said Modi, adding he would interact with the vibrant Indian community in the Philippines, whose contributions strengthen the bonds between the two countries. Modi will also have a bilateral meeting with Marcos on the margins of the multilateral events, before returning to India late Tuesday.The meeting that will likely draw maximum attention in India and possibly Japan is the Quad leaders' summit - the first such meeting since Trump returned to the White House. Amid speculation that Trump might have downgraded Quad, the summit is expected to reaffirm commitment, if not announce fresh initiatives, in shared areas of interest like maritime security, critical technologies, supply chains, connectivity, health and economic security.The US said ahead of the meeting that the "partnership of action" will focus on shared interests of peace, prosperity and security in the Indo-Pacific region. As Trump heads into a "groundbreaking" trilateral summit with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, respectively, in Shenzhen, it'll be interesting to see if he tones down Quad rhetoric on China or modulates messaging on South and East China Seas.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Nigeria's education crisis: Why millions of children can't go to school
articles.summary: BBC World Service launches programme in Hausa for out-of-school children in West Africa.
articles.body:
As she pounds millet, 15-year-old Hadiza sings the English alphabet. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school.

"Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says.

One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village.

"They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We had to run away. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says.

Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home. For a short while she went to school here, but soon met a young man and, at the age of 13, stopped going to classes and got married.

"It's tradition here that once a girl is married, her education ends," she explains.

Now she lives with her in-laws and helps look after the home.

Although Nigerian law prohibits marriage under the age of 18, it is not always enforced.

Hadiza is one of nearly 19 million children in Nigeria who are missing out on an education, according to estimates shared by Unesco in 2024. That's about one in four of the country's school-age children.

Against this backdrop, the BBC World Service has launched Dars Hausa, an educational programme in the main language spoken in northern Nigeria, as well as neighbouring Niger, Cameroon and elsewhere in West Africa.

It brings English, maths and science lessons to children across West Africa, via social media, local television partnerships and radio. Many people in the region get their news from the radio and nearly half of households in Nigeria have one, according to the charity Save the Children.

Dars means "lesson" in Pashto and Dari, and it was first launched in those languages in 2023 for Afghan children barred from attending school. An Arabic version followed in February 2025.

The reasons why so many Nigerian children are out of school are numerous and complex. Like Hadiza, 12-year-old Rukayya also lives in the displacement camp in Goronyo.

"It pains me to see other children studying and going to school while I cannot," she says.

As the eldest child, each day Rukayya goes out to gather firewood to sell and to beg so that her younger siblings can have something to eat.

"If my father was alive, I wouldn't have to go out and beg," she explains, saying some people mock her "but it doesn't stop me because it is our only way to survive."

Bandits killed her father about a year ago in front of her, she says, and her family fled from their home to the camp.

She and Hadiza are among 670,000 people in north-west and central Nigeria who have been forced from their homes by armed robbery and kidnappings, according to the International Organization for Migration.

Three Girls: Lessons in Limbo features the stories of Hadiza and Rukayya - you can watch the full film on YouTube

Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by criminal gangs, known in Nigeria as bandits, who steal, kill and kidnap.

The school that Hadiza once attended in Goronyo is the only one serving children in the camp and typically has about 50 students in each class.

One of the teachers, Kamilu Sulaiman Jakada, says that even though lessons are free, only a tiny portion of the children attend, and even then sporadically, because parents tell him that "it is the children that are the breadwinners" and they need to earn money to eat.

He says the school does not have enough teachers or classrooms, explaining that funding is inconsistent and often comes from individuals or organisations rather than the government.

The other challenge is the bandits. A gang once came to the school on motorbikes, shooting in the air, he says, and although no-one was hurt, many parents were scared and withdrew their children. That has been parents' reaction to attacks in some other parts of the country too.

Every Nigerian child is meant to get nine years of free, compulsory education - six in primary and three in secondary school. Responsibility is shared between federal, state and local governments.

But many schools are facing shortages and poorer families who cannot afford private education can struggle to pay for uniforms, books and transport.

The crisis has built up over decades, with successive governments struggling to address chronic underfunding and poor oversight of resources.

In addition, many children in the traditional Almajiri system, which provides Islamic education, are not taught subjects such as maths and science, and are considered by Unicef to be out of school.

Minister of State for Education Prof Suwaiba Sa'id believes the number of children out of school is lower than has been reported, but admits that with Nigeria's growing population "the proper investment, the proper oversight, has not been done… I will not mention the names, but we know of two states that did not recruit a single teacher for eight years".

She says that education is the government's "number-one priority" and initiatives such as Lumina are designed to help address "decades of neglect". Lumina aims to support one million girls by 2030, providing an accelerated learning programme for older girls who have missed years of formal education.

She also says that "the government is doing everything possible" to deal with bandits and that "we have seen children that should be at school but are engaged in this banditry".

In the meantime, it is children like Hadiza and Rukayya that the BBC World Service Dars Hausa programmes aim to help. Hadiza says she still has a dream to one day become a doctor "to help my fellow women".

Dars Hausa will air on BBC News Hausa radio on Sundays at 06:45 West Africa Time, with a repeat at 20:45. The programme will also be available via BBC News Hausa's digital platforms, including YouTube, Facebook, X and Instagram.

articles.title: UK weather: Met Office yellow warning in place as snow could disrupt rush hour travel
articles.summary: Snow could bring some transport disruption to the hills of northern England and southern Scotland, as Chris Fawkes explains.
articles.body:
Parts of northern England and southern Scotland are set to get an early taste of winter as hill snow moves in on Tuesday.

A Met Office yellow warning for snow is valid until midday Tuesday with 5-15cm expected at some locations above 300-400m.

Major routes like the A74(M), A66 and M62 could all have problems with transport disruption.

Some railways are also likely to be affected with longer journey times for train services.

Cold health alerts are also in place , external for northern England issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) until 09:00 GMT on Thursday.

A weather front is pushing north and east across the UK bringing a spell of rain to many areas. As this rain reaches northern England it will encounter a reservoir of colder and drier air.

Some of the rain will evaporate in this drier air, which will cool the atmosphere further by a process known as evaporative cooling - the same process involved in cooling your body down when you sweat.

Eventually rain will start to turn to snow, initially over higher hills in the Pennines, moving to lower hills with time. As the precipitation moves northwards and eastwards, the snow will spread to the Cumbrian hills and into Scotland's Southern Uplands.

The snow will come down in big, wet, chunky flakes which could stick to powerlines and tree branches.

The extra weight of the snow combined with wind gusts of 40-50mph over high ground could bring down tree branches and powerlines, bringing an additional risk of some localised power cuts.

Heating tips to keep your home warm when budgets are squeezed

How to keep babies warm in cold weather and other winter tips

Some snow may accumulate down to 100m elevation or so, with around 1-5cm possible.

Any snow will probably be quite short-lived, turning back to rain by 09:00 in most parts.

Cold outbreaks of rain will be left across northern areas of the UK through Tuesday afternoon with some hill fog and a chilly wind.

Meanwhile the south will have sunshine and blustery showers but it will also turn milder with temperatures up to 14C.

Rain and showers will continue to impact Northern Ireland, England and Wales for the next few days.

There will still be some rain in Scotland on Wednesday but then high pressure will take over with sunnier weather returning.

This drier, sunnier weather will then push southwards across most of the UK by the end of the week with cold air returning, along with some overnight frosts and a few coastal showers.

You can keep up to date with your local forecast by checking BBC Weather online and on the app .

articles.title: Democratic judge under fire for releasing violent offenders calls bail law a ‘direct assault’ on rights
articles.summary: Judge David Carpenter called Alabama’s Aniah’s Law a ‘direct assault’ on constitutional rights, citing defendants’ presumption of innocence.
articles.body: A Democratic Alabama judge facing mounting scrutiny over past decisions to release violent offenders is criticizing a state law that allows defendants charged with certain violent crimes to be denied bail. Circuit Court Judge David Carpenter called Alabama’s Aniah’s Law a direct assault on constitutional rights, arguing that defendants should not be held indefinitely based solely on criminal charges, citing the constitutional presumption of innocence. In a social media post, Carpenter argued that critics of government overreach involving license plate cameras, such as Flock cameras, are not equally concerned about expanded pretrial detention laws. "Can someone explain to me why the people who are so alarmed that a flock camera might spot their car on a public road, and they call that government overreach, are silent on the fact that voters across the country keep overwhelmingly passing new laws to empower the government to hold you in jail indefinitely on the basis of a charge only," Carpenter said. THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC? "These laws, like Alabama’s Aniah’s Law, are a direct assault on the Constitutional guarantee of the presumption of innocence. But no one is talking about this at all, much less expressing the hysteria associated with having a camera see a license plate," he said. Although Aniah’s Law was originally passed in 2022, Alabama voters approved a major constitutional amendment this year expanding the law to cover additional offenses. The expansion added attempted murder, solicitation or conspiracy to commit murder, and discharging a firearm or explosives into an occupied dwelling, building or vehicle. "We are all one accusation away from being a criminal defendant," Carpenter said in a post on Facebook. WHITE HOUSE CALLS DC POLICIES 'INSANITY' AFTER 19-YEAR-OLD GUNMAN GETS PROBATION IN SHOOTING Carpenter has faced controversy over several judicial decisions over the years. Local outlet 1819 News reported that he previously described himself online as a "far left, liberal, progressive, democratic socialist." In April 2023, Carpenter approved a plea deal for Damien McDaniel, who was arrested in 2019 for shooting two people in a car when he was 17 years old, 1819 News reported. After being released from jail, McDaniel allegedly went on a 14-month shooting spree across Alabama, killing 18 people and injuring more than 30 others. Carpenter also granted bond to Raukeem Cunningham in connection with the 2022 shooting death of a teenage girl, the outlet reported. While out on bond, Cunningham was arrested and charged with fatally shooting three people at a Bessemer gas station in 2024, prompting the revocation of his original bond. In addition, Carpenter reportedly dismissed a 2015 rape charge against Fredrick Terrenda Hampton in 2019, according to reports. The dismissal came just two days before Hampton met Paighton Houston, who later disappeared. Her body was found buried behind a home after she died of an accidental overdose. CONVICTED SERIAL RAPIST ORIGINALLY SENTENCED TO 124 YEARS WALKS FREE AFTER 20, SPARKING OUTRAGE Hampton pleaded guilty to abuse of a corpse in connection with Houston’s death, and Carpenter gave him a 20-year split sentence with only three years to serve in custody, the outlet said. "If elected, I will work to reduce the number of repeat offenders while addressing the expensive problem of prison overcrowding in Alabama," he said.

articles.title: 5 European countries aim to send rejected asylum seekers to center in Rwanda
articles.summary: VIENNA — A group of European countries announced Monday that they aim to set up a “return hub” in Rwanda where rejected asylum seekers could be sent from next year, a move that they hope will also deter more people from coming.
articles.body: VIENNA — A group of European countries announced Monday that they aim to set up a “return hub” in Rwanda where rejected asylum seekers could be sent from next year, a move that they hope will also deter more people from coming. The European Union has worked for years to tighten migration rules, push down the number of asylum seekers coming to the 27-nation bloc and increase deportations of migrants who aren’t entitled to stay. Sending people to centers outside Europe has emerged as a central plank of that effort. The plan by Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands, which have spearheaded negotiations with non-EU countries, drew immediate criticism from human rights groups. A final agreement is expected within months The aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said alongside officials from the other European countries and Rwanda’s interior minister. “I think this will be a game changer making us able to confront the massive challenges with illegal migration,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said. “We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders and we will remove the incentives for illegal migration.” She predicted that “many other European countries” would join in. Her immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, said that the plan is to have a fully negotiated agreement with Rwanda “within the next few months.” European officials point to a deterrent effect Officials were vague about how many migrants might be sent to Rwanda, but emphasized the plan’s deterrent effect. “The most important number is the number that we will never see because hopefully they will not start their journey to Europe,” Frederiksen said. “So this is a milestone.” Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said that his country would give a “second chance” to people who have no right to stay in Europe. He said that those who arrive will be offered the opportunity “to voluntarily return to the countries of origin, integrate into Rwandan society or relocate to another destination where they have the legal right to reside, according to their preference.” Asked how Rwanda would guarantee refugees’ human rights, he said that Rwanda would bring on board organizations such as the U.N. refugee agency and “there will be an independent monitoring mechanism.” Human rights groups criticize plans for facilities in third countries Human rights groups have criticized plans to deport migrants to facilities in third countries, arguing that European nations can’t guarantee that their rights will be respected there. European officials insist that the new hubs would abide by European and international law. “Offshore deportation centers are the latest cynical expression of the EU’s drive to shift its responsibilities to other countries,” Human Rights Watch researcher Clementine de Montjoye said in a statement. “Paying Kigali to host a deportation program would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad.” Amnesty International Austria asylum and migration expert Aimée Stuflesser said in a statement that “today’s disgraceful deportation deal between European countries and Rwanda repeats mistakes of the past.” “Sending people to a country they have never been to is irresponsible and there is a real danger that the Rwanda deal will, with its limited chance for scrutiny, become a cruel black hole for human rights,” Stuflesser said. The U.N. refugee agency said that it only supports the possible use of return hubs in line with human rights standards, and as a way to help returns of people whose claims for asylum were denied after a full and fair assessment. UNHCR spokesperson Matthew Saltmarsh said that the agency was involved in “constructive discussions” with the five EU countries “to provide advice on the compliance of the return hub process with international human rights law standards.” No agreement with the countries has been signed. The U.N.’s International Organization for Migration said that it doesn’t take part in or negotiate “state-to-state removal arrangements,” but was providing “technical input on the return hub process.” IOM said that it was prepared to provide help to migrants at the request of the receiving government if “necessary safeguards” are in place. EU laws have changed in recent years because of persistent public and political pressure for tougher measures against migration. European lawmakers voted in June to allow member states to set up centers outside the EU on their own or in small coalitions, and send rejected asylum seekers there instead of to their home countries. Europeans say plan isn’t comparable to scrapped U.K. deal Rwanda struck a deal with the U.K. in 2022 under which migrants who arrived as stowaways or in boats would be sent to the African nation, where their asylum claims would be processed and, if successful, they would stay. The U.K. Supreme Court ruled that the policy was unlawful because Rwanda isn’t a safe third country for migrants sent there. Then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer scrapped that deal immediately after taking office in 2024. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Monday that the European plan for Rwanda isn’t comparable. He said that the U.K. had planned to outsource asylum proceedings to third countries, while the European plan involves people who have been through the asylum process and exhausted their appeals.
