articles.title: Failed asylum seekers face removal without five-day notice period
articles.summary: Under proposed new rules, the Home Office would have six months in which to remove a person without telling them in advance.
articles.body:
The government is to change the law so that it no longer has to give failed asylum seekers notice before they are removed from the country.

Currently, people are given five working days' notice but ministers believe this leads to last-minute appeals which delay the process.

Under the new rules, once an asylum claim fails, the Home Office would have six months in which to remove the applicant without telling them in advance.

The move was criticised by the Refugee Council which said: "Removing people at such short notice will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety to people."

Imran Hussain, the director of the refugee charity, said: "The reality is that voluntary removals are far more effective at removing people than enforced returns.

"If you assist people to return with dignity, many will take that option, at far lower cost to the taxpayer."

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood will make the change by amending the Immigration and Asylum Bill which is currently going through Parliament.

The amendment will scrap the notice requirement for those who have exhausted the asylum appeals process.

Instead, the Home Office will have the power to remove people immediately, a power that will remain in place for up to six months.

The Home Office has not said how many additional people it thinks it will be able to remove but has pointed to Denmark where the number of migrants awaiting removal more than halved over five years to under 1,000 after a similar policy was introduced.

The previous government, led by Sir Keir Starmer, had pledged to clear the asylum backlog.

In June 2026, there were 40,168 people waiting for an initial decision on asylum application claims and a further 90,341 waiting for the outcome of an appeal in the courts.

Between July 2025 and June 2026, 38% of asylum decisions led to the applicant being granted refugee status.

Forty percent of all asylum claims come from people who arrived in the UK by small boat.

The remaining 60% of claims are made by people who arrived in the country by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and subsequently applied for asylum.

Anna Turley, minister for border security and asylum, said: "We are ensuring those migrants who have exhausted their right to appeal can be removed promptly, rather than being given an opportunity to frustrate their legitimate removal from this country.

"This bill will restore order and control to the system, ensuring it is swift and fair."

articles.title: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
articles.summary: Pakistan's ex-prime minister, who has been in prison since August 2023, says he has been denied justice.
articles.body:
Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating.

"At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive," the cricket star-turned-politician wrote in a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar.

Authorities in Islamabad maintain that Khan gets seen weekly by doctors, who have assessed that he is of "satisfactory" health.

Khan, who faces more than 100 charges, has been in prison since August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Khan argues the cases against them, ranging from corruption to selling state gifts, are politically motivated.

Concerns over Khan's health have grown louder in the past year, with his family claiming he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.

In his letter, Khan wrote that doctors have told him he is "highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest", and that his heart has already "suffered damage".

He also expressed concern for Bushra Bibi, whom he says suffered a detached retina in April and underwent surgery in secrecy. Khan said he fears she may lose her sight without further surgery.

"I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice," he wrote.

He said that he is being held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day, where he is allowed neither visits by his family nor access to books and television, and that this has "taken a heavy toll" on his mental health.

He also claimed he had only seen his lawyers four times over the past year.

"I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he wrote.

Pakistan's parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed these claims, saying Khan is "provided with all facilities in prison, including food of his own choosing".

"[He] is currently the most well-accommodated prisoner in Pakistan," the minister told reporters.

Authorities also say Khan was taken to a government-run hospital for an eye injection a week ago, where doctors deemed him "clinically stable".

Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.

His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.

At least eight people died in the protests and the army were called in to quell the violence.

Even behind bars, Khan remains a force in Pakistani politics.

Thousands of his supporters took to the streets in early October in a dayslong march , demanding his release. Authorities later ordered a crackdown on protests and imposed a state of emergency in Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, insisting that Khan be given proper medical care.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial in March 2027 after Judge rejects double jeopardy challenge
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of killing her three young children, will face a retrial in March next year after a jury failed to reach a
articles.body: Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of killing her three young children, will face a retrial in March next year after a jury failed to reach a verdict in her first trial.Judge William Sullivan set March 29, 2027, as the trial date during a hearing on Monday, BBC reported.However, the district attorney's office has not formally confirmed which charges Clancy, 36, will face in the retrial.Prosecutors said they wanted the case to be heard by a jury, which the defence interpreted as an indication that the prosecution intended to pursue the original first-degree murder charges. Defence lawyer Kevin Reddington said the district attorney's position had not been explicitly stated."I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA [district attorney] that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments, so we will pick a trial date," Reddington said at Monday's hearing, as per the BBC.Prosecutors had sought a May trial date, but Sullivan opted for March. The judge is due to retire in June.Clancy was charged with three counts of first-degree murder in the original trial. The charge applies to intentional and premeditated killings. The district attorney has not yet officially confirmed whether he will pursue the same charges in the retrial. Prosecutors could also opt for lesser charges, including second-degree murder, which applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness but without premeditation.Defence argues Clancy suffered from postpartum psychosisClancy's three children, five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson and eight-month-old Callan, were strangled at the family's home in Duxbury, a suburb of Boston, on January 24, 2023.It was not disputed during the first trial that Clancy strangled the children with exercise bands in the basement of the family home. Shortly before the attack, she had asked her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, to leave the house to collect takeaway food and medicine for the children.The defence argued that Clancy was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis and should be found not guilty by reason of insanity, a legal defence known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.Clancy is currently being held at a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts.Judge rejects double jeopardy challengeThe retrial will proceed after Sullivan rejected a defence attempt last week to have the case dismissed on double jeopardy grounds, BBC reported.Double jeopardy is a legal principle that protects a person from being prosecuted again for the same crime after an acquittal or conviction.Sullivan had declared a mistrial on September 4 after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict.Following the mistrial, some of the 12 jurors told media outlets that they had been prepared to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, but that one juror had refused to agree.The case has drawn widespread attention and prompted debate in the United States over the treatment of postpartum mental illness.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mustard oil, coconut oil, or no oil at all: What actually helps your hair in winter?
articles.summary: Winters are almost here, and so are the dryness and itchiness of the hair and scalp.
articles.body: Winters are almost here, and so are the dryness and itchiness of the hair and scalp.And as soon as the hair feels frizzy or the scalp starts acting dry, the most common solution in Indian households is a warm bowl of oil thoroughly massaged into the scalp.In North India, that oil is usually mustard. Along the coasts and in the south, it is coconut. And lately, social media has added a third category that advises skipping oil altogether because it only makes hair greasy and attracts dust.But what exactly is the right choice?Amid the chilly season, which is quite hard on hair. Cold air outside and dry, heated air indoors pull moisture out of the strands and the scalp, which can leave hair brittle, frizzy, full of static charge, and the scalp flaky.But does oiling the hair always protect from damage?Is there actually any evidence, or do we do it just as a habit?Let’s see what science has to sayMustard oil, coconut oil or no oil: what actually is the right choice for your hair in winter?Researchers compared coconut, sunflower and mineral oil on hair tresses in a 2003 study published in the Journal of Cosmetic Science. According to the paper, coconut oil was "the only oil found to reduce the protein loss remarkably" in both undamaged and damaged hair.The authors associate this to its structure, as coconut oil has a low molecular weight and penetrates the hair's cortex, while mineral oil does not penetrate at all. Sunflower oil's bulky structure also keeps it out of the fibre. Less protein loss means less breakage, which is crucial when winter air has already made hair brittle.How does Mustard oil impact the hair?A 2022 review in the International Journal of Trichology says it inhibits fungal penetration of hair, but less effectively than coconut and amla oil; these findings come from lab work, often on plant extracts, not clinical trials. It may help with dryness-related flaking, but it has not been shown to treat dandruff.What does this mean in winter?The scalp dries out in cold weather, and according to the Cleveland Clinic, an oil or conditioner can keep it moisturised. So an oil massage can help provide moisture, and even though Mustard oil has a warming effect, it is not proven to be better than other options.What about no oil at all?Oil is an option to keep the hair moisture intact and prevent dryness, but it is not the only one. Cleveland Clinic dermatologist Dr Wilma Bergfeld advises, "You should treat your hair like a cashmere sweater." In practice, that means less heat styling, gentle brushing, and waiting to comb until wet hair is less damp.So what should you do?For dry or damaged hair: coconut oil on the lengths before washing is the best-supported choice.For dry, itchy scalp, and you like mustard oil: use a small amount, diluted, after a patch test.For oily scalp or sensitive skin: skipping oil and conditioning the ends is fine.For red, painful or stubborn flaking: see a dermatologist instead of adding more oil.You use AI every day.
